summary: This Best Current Practice describes an architecture for location information in Internet applications, including privacy. It covers how to gather and transfer location securely while protecting individuals, with rules attached to the data.

plainLanguage.summary: Geopriv describes how Internet applications can share location information together with rules about who may receive it and how it may be used. Those rules inform recipients, but the architecture cannot technically force them to comply.

questions: how does location privacy work on the internet
subtitle: An architecture for sharing location information with privacy rules attached.

tldr.problem: Internet applications need location data, but location can expose sensitive details about a person's movements and recipients may not know how the owner wants it used.
tldr.mechanism: Geopriv defines roles for creating, distributing, and receiving location, plus a Location Object that carries location data and privacy rules. Rules grant permission, and the default is to deny access.
tldr.outcome: The architecture informs recipients of the owner's rules, but does not technically guarantee that they follow them. RFC 6280 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 3693 and RFC 3694.

facts.label: Geopriv roles
facts.value: Target, Device, Rule Maker, Location Generator, Location Server, Location Recipient

facts.label: Default rule policy
facts.value: Deny unless a rule grants permission

sections.title: Why Location Needs Special Care
sections.content:
Navigation, emergency services, friend finders, and equipment tracking may need the location of a person or device. Location can also reveal sensitive facts, such as a visit to a medical clinic or patterns of movement.

The Geopriv architecture uses a Location Object to carry location information together with user-specified privacy rules. Those rules are intended to remain associated with the location as it is shared.
sections.plainLanguage: Location can reveal where a person has been and what they may be doing. Geopriv keeps the owner's sharing rules with the location information.

sections.title: Binding Privacy Rules to Location Data
sections.content:
Geopriv shifts the privacy model so the person whose location is described can express preferences about its use. Rules may limit who receives the data, how precise it is, whether it can be retransmitted, or how long it can be retained.

Geopriv does not technically guarantee that recipients follow the rules. Its design makes recipients aware of the rules, which can support enforcement through legal, contractual, or consumer-protection processes.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules tell recipients what the location owner permits. The system does not stop a recipient from breaking those rules, but it makes the recipient aware of them.

sections.title: Roles and Data Formats
sections.content:
The architecture defines a Target, Device, Rule Maker, Location Generator, Location Server, and Location Recipient. The Target is the person or object whose privacy is protected. The Device is tracked as its proxy; a Rule Maker creates rules; a Location Generator determines location; a Location Server applies rules and distributes data; and a Location Recipient receives it.

A Location Object carries geodetic or civic location data with privacy rules. One organization or device may perform several roles.
sections.plainLanguage: Geopriv separates the person being located, the device, the rule maker, the location source, the distributor, and the recipient. A single system can perform more than one role.

sections.title: The Location Life Cycle
sections.content:
Location passes through positioning, distribution, and use. During positioning, a Location Generator determines the Device's location. During distribution, Location Servers provide it to recipients, who may pass it on if the rules permit. During use, a recipient acts on the location.

Positioning may be device-based, network-based, or network-assisted. Protocols carrying positioning data MUST provide confidentiality and integrity protection. Local identifiers or unlinked pseudonyms should be used where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Location first gets determined, then may be distributed, and finally is used by a recipient. Each stage has different privacy and security needs.

sections.title: Default-Deny Rules and Distribution
sections.content:
Privacy rules follow a default-deny pattern. An empty rule set denies requests except those from the Target itself; each rule grants a specific permission. A Location Server can enforce rules by refusing a request or transforming the location, such as returning a less precise value.

Local Rules stay within the Location Server. Forwarded Rules travel with the Location Object, but only the subset needed by the next recipient should be sent because rules can reveal sensitive information too.
sections.plainLanguage: If no rule grants permission, the Location Server denies access. It can also reduce the detail in a location before sharing it.

sections.title: Combining Rule Sets
sections.content:
A Location Server must accept rules only from authorized Rule Makers and combine all rules that apply before distributing a Location Object. If an object contains no rules authorizing further transmission, the server MUST NOT retransmit it; if it contains no rules at all, the server MUST delete it.

The default when combining multiple rule sources is Union: a transmission is allowed if either source grants it. Intersection requires both sources to permit it and is the most restrictive of the listed example policies.
sections.plainLanguage: A Location Server checks every applicable rule before sharing location. The default combination policy accepts a permission from either rule source, while Intersection requires both sources to permit sharing.

sections.title: Security Across the Location Life Cycle
sections.content:
Protocols carrying Location Objects and privacy rules MUST support mutual authentication and message integrity. Location Objects SHOULD have end-to-end confidentiality. A secure transport protects a single connection segment; a chain of intermediaries requires trust and protection at each segment.

A Location Object binds the Target's identity, location, time, and rules. Security mechanisms must protect these associations against falsified locations, altered timestamps, fake identities, replay, and rule tampering. Passing location by reference can reduce a multi-hop path to a single retrieval transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: Security must protect both the location data and its connection to the Target, time, and rules. A secure connection protects one step in the distribution chain, not every earlier step.
